objectives.label: Read the glassback crab's warning before anybody got pinched
Found the cold cinder wolves something to eat
Listened to the soup-tent woman all the way through

facet_table.name: The Table Stone
facet_table.text: From the Redspire truth-table. Logged twice. Hums whenever someone tells the truth.

scene_arrival.narration: The foothills smell like warm rocks and burnt toast. The rush has run out of road up here: tents on every ledge, claim flags on every boulder, and a dragonling grandmother ringing a hand bell at a man who is trying to dig up her doorstep. He is losing.

choices.label: Walk up into the foothills
Come down from the broken bridge, in the northeast
Step off the bigfoot high paths, in the west
Walk up through the boundary stones, in the south

scene_door_river.narration: You come down off the cracked bridge with the wardens' engineers, who are still arguing about one crack in particular. From up here the whole road home is laid out behind you: the bridge, the bent pride roads, the river where the trolls still ask their question. All of it leans toward the mountain, the way grass leans in a wind.

choices.label: Down into the camps

scene_door_wild.narration: The bigfoot high paths end at a mossy step that drops straight into ash. A MossHome runner coming the other way waves, and does not take one step onto the ash. The moss stops exactly where the ash starts, as if somebody drew the line with a ruler and the forest agreed to keep to it.

choices.label: Step down into the ash

scene_door_rush.narration: You walk up the caravan road from the boundary stones, in the middle of a crowd that has no idea it just crossed anything. The grandmothers ring a bell for every pick that passes. They are ringing a lot. One of them has switched to a smaller bell to save her arm.

choices.label: Up into the camps

scene_doorstep.narration: The man with the pick is called Dunmore, and he has planted his claim flag right on the grandmother's front step. "It hums!" he says, pointing. It does hum. So does every stone up here. The grandmother rings her bell at him again, louder. Dunmore goes pink to the ears, but he does not let go of the pick.

choices.label: Talk Dunmore out of digging up somebody's house
Help him find a humming rock that is nobody's door
Say the one rule, the way grandmothers say it

check_doorstep.prompt: Talk Dunmore down off the grandmother's doorstep

onSuccess.narration: You tell Dunmore that a house is a house, even when it hums. He looks at the step, then at the little round window with curtains in it, and goes pinker than ever. "Sorry," he mumbles, and pulls up his flag. The grandmother gives him a biscuit. He is so surprised that he says thank you twice.

onFailure.narration: Dunmore does not hear a word, because the grandmother has started ringing her bell right beside his ear. In the end he gives up on the step just to get away from the noise, and stomps off up the slope, rubbing his ear and grumbling about bells.

scene_doorstep_dig_elsewhere.narration: You walk Dunmore up the slope until you find a big humming boulder with nobody's door in it. He plants his flag on top, very proud. The grandmother rings her bell once, sweetly, which means thank you. Dunmore waves goodbye for a long time. He is the sort of man who keeps waving after everybody else has stopped.

choices.label: Walk on up into the foothills

scene_doorstep_one_rule.narration: Your dragonling stands on the step and says it, the way it is said at every dragonling door: "Take what the mountain drops. Never pry at what it holds." Dunmore takes off his hat. "Nobody told me there were rules," he says, very quietly. The grandmother tells him there have always been rules. He writes them on the inside of his hat.

choices.label: Walk on up into the foothills

scene_moths.narration: Embermoths are supposed to crowd toward warm cracks. Today every one of them is sitting on the cold side of a rock, shivering. One has landed in a prospector's soup and will not leave, because the soup is the only warm thing it still trusts, and the prospector has given up and is eating around it.

choices.label: Follow the moths' line down the slope
Carry the soup moth back to a warm crack
Say it out loud: moths leaving the warm is a warning
Count the moths. All of them.

scene_moths_follow.narration: You follow the moths down the slope. They are not scattered at all. They sit in a line, rock after rock, every one facing the same way, like an arrow somebody drew pointing away from the mountain. At the bottom of the arrow is the caravan road, and in the ruts of the road, something is glowing.

choices.label: Go and see what's glowing

scene_moths_coax.narration: You lift the soup moth out, very gently, and carry it to the warmest crack on the slope. It sits there for one breath. Then it walks, on its tiny feet, straight back out to the cold side of the rock, and looks at you as if you had asked it to sit in an oven. The prospector gets his soup back, and says thank you with his mouth full.

choices.label: Follow the moths down to the road

scene_moths_count.narration: Your bigfoot counts them. All of them. It takes a while, and the prospector with the moth in his soup gets quite impatient. Three hundred and twelve embermoths, and every single one is facing away from the mountain, like an audience that has turned its back on the stage.

choices.label: Follow the moths' line down the slope

scene_moths_say_it.narration: "Moths leaving the warm is a warning," says your dragonling, out loud, in the voice grandmothers use. A grandmother three tents away hears it, stops in the middle of an argument, and rings her hand bell once, sharp, toward the next town. Then she goes back to arguing with a different man on her own doorstep. He has not moved. Neither have the moths.

choices.label: Follow the moths' line down the slope

scene_wolves.narration: Down on the caravan road, a pack of cinder wolves is lying in one big heap in the ruts, glowing faintly, like a pile of coals with ears. They are not hunting. They are cold and hungry, and forty wagons are stuck behind them, with forty drovers yelling.

choices.label: Find them something easier to eat than a traffic jam
Fly up and look for what they could eat instead
Wait for them to move on

scene_wolves_wait.narration: You sit on a rock and wait. The drovers yell. The wolves do not care. After an hour the pack gets up, all at once, stretches, and trots off downhill as if that had always been the plan. Forty wagons start moving. Forty drovers decide it was their doing.

choices.label: Up the road, toward a smell of soup

scene_wolves_fly_look.narration: From the air you see it at once: a sausage cart tipped on its side in the ditch, a hundred paces down, with the drover long gone. You come down low over the wolves and fly a slow, obvious line toward it. The biggest wolf lifts its nose, understands you perfectly, and the whole pack flows out of the ruts after it like water finding a drain.

choices.label: Up the road, toward a smell of soup

check_wolves.prompt: Find the hungry wolves something better than the road

onSuccess.narration: You spot an overturned sausage cart in the ditch. The wolves spot it two seconds after you. The road clears in a hurry, and one wolf looks back at you as if it is memorizing your face.

onFailure.narration: Your plan involves a sausage on a string, and the wolves are not impressed. In the end they wander off on their own, howling long complaints at the mountain.

scene_claim_boulder.narration: Halfway up the road, below a soup tent you can already smell from here, two prospectors are standing back to back on one boulder, each holding a claim flag. The boulder hums. "Mine," says one. "Mine," says the other. They have been saying it since breakfast, and they have each tied a bootlace round the boulder so nobody can push them off. A crowd has brought snacks.

choices.label: Work out whose flag went in first
Tell them to share it, half each
Turn the argument into a show for the crowd
Show them the Unassigned Stone: some stones are nobody's

check_claim.prompt: Find out whose claim flag went into the boulder first

onSuccess.narration: You check the flag holes. Both are brand new. But under the moss at the bottom of the boulder is a third mark, a little carved line, so old the moss has grown into it. It was here before either of them. It was here before anyone. Both prospectors stare at it, untie their bootlaces, and go and find a different boulder, quietly.

onFailure.narration: You measure the flags, count the footprints, and ask the crowd. Everybody gives a different answer, and two people give three. In the end the boulder settles it by humming so loudly that both prospectors hop off at once, and neither of them wants to get back on.

scene_claim_boulder_share.narration: "Half each," you say. Both prospectors look at the boulder, which is round, and then at each other. They draw a chalk line down the middle. Then they argue for a while about whose half the hum is in. But they are sitting down while they argue, which is progress, and somebody in the crowd claps.

choices.label: Up the road to the soup tent

scene_claim_boulder_show.narration: Your kitsune jumps up beside them and turns the argument into a play, with voices. The crowd laughs, then cheers, then votes. The winner gets the boulder. The loser gets everybody's snacks, which turns out to be a much better prize. By the end, the winner is trying to swap.

choices.label: Up the road to the soup tent

scene_claim_boulder_nobodys.narration: You hold up the Unassigned Stone and tell them about the grandmothers' very old list: the caves that are never given to anybody, not ever. The two prospectors look at it for a long time. "Nobody's," says one, trying out the word. "Nobody's," agrees the other. They leave the boulder where it is and go and share a sandwich instead.

choices.label: Up the road to the soup tent

scene_soup_tent.narration: At the top of the road is a soup tent with a sign: FREE, NO QUESTIONS. A woman called Hessa Wren ladles you each a bowl, asks your names, and remembers them. "The world's laws are broken," she says kindly, as if she were telling you it might rain. "That seal on the mountain isn't protecting anyone. It's a cage on the cure."

choices.label: Ask her what the cure would fix
Say no thank you, kindly but clearly
Just eat the soup
Notice the mask folded in her apron pocket, and ask about it
Tell her you remember Wend's soup tents on the road north

scene_soup_tent_ford_soup.narration: "Wend's tents, on the north road!" Hessa's face lights up. "Wend sends love. Wend sends love to everybody, but Wend did say your names." She ladles an extra spoonful into each bowl. It is the same soup. It tastes, oddly, like the whole road north.

choices.label: Find somewhere warm to sleep

scene_soup_tent_mask.narration: Your kitsune nods at the painted bark mask folded in her apron pocket. Hessa does not hide it. "For singing in," she says. "The mountain likes a choir." She hums three notes, and the humming stones in your packs hum back before you can stop them. She smiles at that like a gardener at a seedling.

choices.label: Find somewhere warm to sleep

scene_soup_tent_just_soup.narration: You just eat the soup. It is excellent soup, with barley in it and something green. Hessa watches you eat with a look that is mostly kindness and partly patience, and when you hand the bowls back she says, "Tomorrow, then," as if you had an appointment.

choices.label: Find somewhere warm to sleep

scene_soup_tent_no_thanks.narration: "No, thank you," you say, kindly and clearly. Hessa does not argue, and she does not stop smiling, and she does not take the bowl back. "The soup isn't the pitch," she says. "The soup is just soup." You believe her about the soup.

choices.label: Find somewhere warm to sleep

scene_soup_tent_ask_cure.narration: "What would it fix?" Hessa thinks about it properly, which not everyone does. "Who gets to be hungry," she says at last. "Who gets to be cold. Why the sky is the wrong color and nobody with a ledger can say why." She refills your bowl. "Little things," she says. "Everything."

choices.label: Find somewhere warm to sleep

rest_warm_stones.narration: A dragonling town lets you sleep on the warming-stones by its doors, which are exactly as cozy as they sound. Grandmother Tull rings the night bell, the ordinary one, and says the other ring, the one nobody uses, is nothing to worry about. She says it twice. Share out your things, patch each other up, and sleep.

choices.label: In the morning, see what the bells are doing

scene_morning_bells.narration: In the morning, Grandmother Tull is teaching the bell code to a row of very small dragonlings, each with a very small bell. One ring for breakfast. Two for visitors. Three for lost goats. On the top shelf sits one more bell, wrapped up tight in a woolly sock. "Nothing to worry about," says Grandmother Tull, before anybody asks. High above the town, at the top of the ridge, stands a black tower: Redspire Citadel, where the Skywardens keep their records.

choices.label: Sit on the bench and learn the morning ring
Ask about the bell in the sock
Fly the morning ring up the ridge to the next town

check_bells.prompt: Ring the morning ring in time with the little dragonlings

onSuccess.narration: Ding, ding-ding, ding. You get it right, and the smallest dragonling gives you a solemn nod, as if you had joined something important. Grandmother Tull presses a warm honeycake into your hands for the climb, and tells you the ridge is that way, as if you might have forgotten.

onFailure.narration: Your ring comes out ding, dong, clatter, which in bell code means, as far as anyone can tell, goats, but sideways. The little dragonlings laugh so hard that one falls off the bench. Grandmother Tull says you will get it next time, and points you up the ridge.

scene_morning_bells_sock.narration: Grandmother Tull takes a long breath. "That one has never been rung," she says. "Not by me. Not by my grandmother. Everybody knows what it would mean, and nobody says it." She pats the sock, the way you pat a sleeping dog. "Nothing to worry about." That is four times now, and this time she does not quite look at you.

choices.label: Climb the ridge toward the citadel

scene_morning_bells_fly_ring.narration: You carry a little bell up the ridge and ring it, one, two-two, one, over the next town. Far below, a whole row of tiny bells rings back, very proudly and not quite together. From up here you can see the citadel's black tower, and halfway up the ridge, a crowd gathered round something that glitters.

choices.label: Glide back down and lead the climb

scene_crab.narration: Halfway up the ridge, a crowd has gathered around a glittering heap of gems. It is Dunmore again, of course, raising his pick at it. The gem heap has eyes. The gem heap has very large claws. It is a glassback crab, and it is lifting both claws high and rocking from side to side.

choices.label: Read what the crab is trying to say
Knock on its burrow stone, and wait
Call to Dunmore by name. He listens to you now.
Pull Dunmore back and face the crab
Back everyone off its warm ground, go the long way

scene_crab_dunmore.narration: "Dunmore!" you call. He knows your voice now, and he stops mid-swing. "Three big steps back." He does it at once, without one word of argument, and the whole crowd steps back with him. The crab lowers its claws, looks Dunmore up and down, and goes back to tidying its pebbles.

choices.label: See what the crab does next

check_crab.prompt: Read the glassback crab's threat display

onSuccess.narration: Two claws up and a rock to the left means: this is my warm ground, and you are standing in my garden. You tell everybody to take three big steps back. The crab lowers its claws and goes back to tidying its pebbles, very pleased.

onFailure.narration: Two claws up and a rock to the left means... you guess "hello." It does not mean hello. The crab charges, and its neighbor from the next burrow scuttles over to see what all the fuss is.

encounter_crab.narration: Two glassback crabs clatter down the switchbacks, their shells flashing every color of the gems around them.

onVictory.narration: Both crabs back off onto their own warm ground, and the moment they get there, they forget you ever existed. It took all morning, though. The sun is high by the time you reach the citadel road.

onDefeat.narration: The crabs nudge you, very firmly, all the way down the ridge and off their warm ground, then go back to their gardening. You are fine. You are also at the bottom of the ridge again, and the afternoon is nearly gone.

check_late_gate.prompt: Race the sunset up the ridge before the citadel gate closes

onSuccess.narration: You run the switchbacks two at a time and slide in under the gate as it comes down, with one finger's width to spare.

onFailure.narration: The gate comes down with a BOOM just as you get there. A warden on the wall gives you a sad little shrug. Rules are rules, even for heroes.

scene_crab_thanks.narration: Dunmore lowers his pick and goes rather pink. The crab moves three pebbles in a way that looks a lot like a thank-you note. And at the top of the ridge, the black tower of Redspire Citadel catches the morning sun.

choices.label: Straight up the ridge road, right now
Fly ahead and tell the gate you're coming
Help Dunmore and the crowd find a better spot first

scene_crab_thanks_help_dunmore.narration: You spend the morning finding Dunmore's crowd a patch of warm ground that does not have a crab under it, which turns out to be harder than it sounds, because the crabs got there first everywhere. By the time the last tent is pitched, the sun is high and the citadel road is full of shadows.

choices.label: Up the ridge road at last

scene_crab_thanks_fly_ahead.narration: You fly ahead up the ridge and land on the citadel wall, which is apparently not allowed. The warden on the gate looks up, looks at the ledger in his hand, and sighs. By the time the rest of you reach the top, the gate is already open and a clerk is already waiting with two ledgers.

choices.label: Go in

scene_citadel_gate.narration: Redspire Citadel is a black tower where every single window faces up. Inside, a clerk named Pellam writes your names in a big ledger, then writes them again in a second ledger, just to be sure. "This way," he says. "The captain has a table."

choices.label: Pellam! From the bridge! How are you here first?
Follow Pellam to the table
Ask why every window faces up

scene_citadel_gate_windows.narration: "So we see it first," says Pellam, as if it were obvious. "Whatever the mountain does, a warden is watching, and a warden is writing it down." He points at a narrow stair that winds up and up. "Four hundred years of watching. Most nights the log says nothing." He looks proud. "Nothing is the best thing a log can say."

choices.label: Follow Pellam down the hall

scene_citadel_gate_desk.narration: Halfway down the hall, Pellam stops at a tall desk with a sign: ANYTHING THAT HUMS, LOG IT HERE. Your packs are humming. They have been humming all the way up the ridge. Pellam dips his pen and waits, the way a cat waits by a mouse hole: politely, and forever.

choices.label: Tip out your packs and let him log everything
Ask what the log is for, first
Show him the Clerk's Stone, already tagged at the bridge

scene_citadel_gate_desk_tip_out.narration: You tip everything out: stones, socks, string, and a crust nobody can explain. Pellam logs every stone twice, with a tiny drawing beside each one. Then he hands it all back and stamps the back of your hands in blue ink: LOGGED. "Now you're honest on paper," he says. "The best kind." The ink will not wash off for days.

choices.label: On to the captain's table

scene_citadel_gate_desk_ask_why.narration: Pellam turns the big log round so you can see. Page after page of stones, four hundred years of them: every gem that ever rolled down the mountain, written down, then written down again. "Every one of them went somewhere," he says. "Nobody ever wrote down where." He taps the newest page. It is full. So is the one before it.

choices.label: On to the captain's table

scene_citadel_gate_desk_clerks.narration: Pellam looks at the little tag on the Clerk's Stone, then at the handwriting on it, which is his own. "Logged at the bridge," he breathes. "Carried up. Here." He has to sit down. It is the happiest anyone has ever seen a clerk. He waves you on without opening a single pack, and writes the word HOME next to the stone.

choices.label: On to the captain's table

scene_pellam_again.narration: Pellam does not look up from the second ledger. "The bridge is logged," he says. "The citadel needed logging. I go where the ledgers are." He writes your names a third time, in a very small notebook he keeps for people he has met twice. "Irregular," he says. "Entirely legal. This way. The captain has a table."

choices.label: Follow Pellam down the hall

scene_truth_table.narration: On a long stone table, the wardens have laid out four hundred years of watch-logs, and in the middle of them a gemstone sits humming to itself. Captain Orla Voss folds her arms. "Show us what you found on the road," she says. "Our logs will fill in the rest."

choices.label: Let the wardens read their logs out first
Work it out yourselves before anybody reads a log
Show the troll's question, sash-maps and bridge survey
Show the wounded glades, the path archive and the knot-cord
Show the relay's spiral verses and the boundary tallies
Set Mother Thrum's tuned charm on the table
Point at the one ledger bound in a different color

scene_truth_table_puzzle.prompt: Put the foothills together before the wardens read their logs

onSuccess.narration: You lay the last two days on the table: moths facing away, wolves too cold to hunt, a crab guarding its warm ground, a whole hillside of stones humming one note. "Everything up here is leaning away from the mountain," you say. Captain Voss pushes the oldest log across the table. "So did we," she says. "Four hundred years ago."

onFailure.narration: You lay out the moths, the wolves and the crab, and they go round and round and will not join up. Pellam clears his throat, very kindly, and opens the oldest log. "It took us four hundred years," he says. "You have had two days."

scene_truth_table_odd_ledger.narration: Your bigfoot points at the one ledger bound in a different color, half under the others. Pellam looks as if he has been caught stealing biscuits. "That one's not read," he says. "It's only kept." Captain Voss holds out her hand, and Pellam gives it to her, and the room gets a lot quieter.

choices.label: Watch it all click together

scene_truth_table_rush_clues.narration: You lay out the spiral verses and the boundary-stone tallies, and Pellam lays a watch-log four hundred years old beside them. The grandmothers' tally marks and the relay's new verses curl the same way the old log does, round every place a stone has ever fallen. Captain Voss looks at the three of them side by side for a long time and says nothing, which from her is a great deal.

choices.label: Watch it all click together

scene_truth_table_wild_clues.narration: You lay out the wounded glades, the path archive and the MossHome knot-cord. Pellam runs a finger down the cord, counting knots, goes very pale, and reaches for the oldest log on the table, the one nobody reads. "Well," says Captain Voss. "The forest keeps records too."

choices.label: Watch it all click together

scene_truth_table_river_clues.narration: You lay out the troll's question, the sash-maps and the bridge survey. Captain Voss does not blink. Then Pellam turns a watch-log round and taps a line four hundred years old, in faded ink: WHERE DID YOU GET THAT, AND WHERE IS IT GOING? The trolls have been asking it for a very long time. Nobody at this table ever wrote down an answer.

choices.label: Watch it all click together

scene_whole_truth.narration: Your clues and the wardens' logs click together like a puzzle. The gemstones are pieces of a seal. The seal holds a titan asleep under Mount Red Sky. And the rush is taking the seal apart, one pocket at a time. In the middle of it all, the gemstone on the table hums. The wardens call it the Table Stone, and Pellam has logged it twice. One very old line just says: an old stone gate, far away in a western marsh, hums the same note. Next to it, in three different handwritings: nobody knows why.

choices.label: Ask to carry the Table Stone (Pellam logs it a third time)
Leave the Table Stone where it is, in warden custody

scene_whole_truth_leave_stone.narration: You leave the Table Stone where it is. Captain Voss nods once. "Custody," she says, and Pellam writes CUSTODY beside both earlier entries, so it has now been logged three times without going anywhere. The stone hums on in the middle of the table, as if it had never expected to leave.

choices.label: Hear the captain's plan

scene_whole_truth_take_stone.narration: Pellam logs the Table Stone a third time, under WITH THEM, and slides it across. It is cool, and heavier than it looks, and it hums against your palm the whole time Captain Voss is unrolling her map. Nobody in the room says you cannot have it. Everybody in the room watches you take it.

choices.label: Hear the captain's plan

scene_acceptable_losses.narration: Captain Voss reads everything. She does not argue with a single word of it. Then she unrolls a map, draws circles around three towns, and says "acceptable losses" as calmly as somebody ordering breakfast. The Table Stone hums a little louder, as if it disagrees.

choices.label: Tell her a town is not a number
Hear the whole plan before you say anything
Roar, very politely, at the map

scene_acceptable_losses_polite_roar.narration: Your manticore roars at the map. It is a polite roar, with a please in it, and it still makes the parchment curl up at the corners and every pen in the room roll off its table. Captain Voss waits until the last pen has stopped. Then she flattens the map, picks up a pencil, and redraws one circle so it misses a town.

choices.label: Step over to the window

scene_acceptable_losses_hear_plan.narration: You hear the whole plan before you say anything. Roads closed from the Pinch, the one gap every road squeezes through, all the way down. Three towns emptied, bells and all. Every stone that comes up the mountain confiscated and every one that comes down it stopped. It is careful, and it is honest, and when the captain finishes, the Table Stone is the only thing in the room making a sound.

choices.label: Step over to the window

scene_acceptable_losses_not_a_number.narration: "A town is not a number," you say. Captain Voss looks at the map for a long moment. "No," she says. "It's three numbers. Houses, people, bells." Then, much quieter, so only your table hears: "I know." She does not rub the circles out. She does draw one of them a little smaller.

choices.label: Step over to the window

scene_whole_truth_window.narration: Captain Voss rolls up the map, and Pellam says the record can wait for one cup of tea. From the tall window you can see the whole foothills going dark. Three lights catch your eye: the lantern on Hessa's soup tent, the glitter of the prospectors' camps, and the bell towers of the dragonling towns. Everybody vote. Which do you watch?

choices.label: Hessa's lantern, moving through the camp
The glittering camps, full of stones
The bell towers of the dragonling towns
Look for the wolf that knows you
Look up, the way the windows do
Ring Grandmother Tull's morning ring, very softly

scene_whole_truth_window_soup.narration: Hessa's lantern is the only light that moves. She is carrying soup out to the edge of the camp, to the tents nobody else visits. Wherever she stops, somebody sits up. It looks very kind from up here. It looks very certain, too. Pellam, beside you, writes nothing at all, and keeps watching.

choices.label: Back to the table for the record

scene_whole_truth_window_camps.narration: The camps glitter like a dropped necklace. Every tent has a stone in it, and every stone catches a little firelight. It is the most beautiful thing in the foothills. When you hold very still you can hear it, too: thousands of stones, all humming the same old note, very softly, a long way from home.

choices.label: Back to the table for the record

scene_whole_truth_window_bells.narration: One by one, the dragonling towns ring their night bell, the ordinary one, passed up the dark from town to town like a lantern handed along a line. When the last town rings, they all go quiet together. Captain Voss counts every ring under her breath, and looks a little more relieved at each one.

choices.label: Back to the table for the record

scene_whole_truth_window_wolf.narration: Down on the dark road, one small glow sits apart from its pack, round with sausage, looking up at the citadel. It is the wolf from the road. Cinder wolves do not wave. This one thumps its tail on the ground twice, which is close, and then curls up facing your window.

choices.label: Back to the table for the record

scene_whole_truth_window_look_up.narration: You look up instead, the way the whole citadel does. Over Mount Red Sky the sky is a deep, wrong red, and right at the top the mountain lets out a slow puff of ash, like somebody breathing in their sleep. "Every night for four hundred years," says Pellam softly, "somebody has stood here and written that down. Tonight it's me."

choices.label: Back to the table for the record

scene_whole_truth_window_ring.narration: Ding, ding-ding, ding, very softly, out of the window into the dark. For a moment nothing happens. Then, far below, a very small bell answers: ding, dong, clatter. The smallest dragonling is still up, practicing. Captain Voss turns away from the window so that nobody can see whether she is smiling.

choices.label: Back to the table for the record

scene_ledger.narration: Pellam opens a fresh page and dips his pen. "Before anybody decides anything," he says, "the record. What have you been doing, all this way?" The whole room waits. Even the Table Stone seems to hum more quietly.

choices.label: Tell it plainly, in your own words
Show the harvest sprites' woven medal
Tell how the wounded glade closed up
Say why you really came: somebody had to
Admit the sprites are still talking about you
Set the Glade Stone on the table
Tip out your pockets, Ember Facet first
Say why you really came: to get rich
Ask what the power under the mountain could actually do
Ask who gets to hold that power
Repeat what Hessa said about the cure

scene_reading_restore.narration: Pellam reads it all back and taps the page. "Helping. Fixing. Putting things back where they belong," he says. "That adds up to one word, and the word is return." Captain Voss raises one eyebrow, which for her is practically a parade.

choices.label: Hear the next question

scene_reading_hoard.narration: Pellam reads it back, and the stones in your packs hum along with every line. "Pockets," he says. "A great many pockets. That adds up to a collection." Nobody in the room says he is wrong. A moth lands on your bag, thinks about it, and leaves.

choices.label: Hear the next question

scene_reading_leash.narration: Pellam reads it back slowly. "Questions about what the power could do. Who holds it. What it's for." He writes one word and underlines it twice: leash. Somewhere below, Hessa's soup tent is still serving.

choices.label: Hear the next question

scene_who_to_tell.narration: "Now," says Captain Voss. "Who else gets to know? Choose carefully. Nobody is going to ask you again."

choices.label: Stand with the wardens' plan
Take it to the grandmothers and the gathering-law towns
Keep it close and tell nobody else
Keep the promise you already made to the wardens
Keep faith with the gatherers you already told
Keep the secret you were already keeping

scene_kept_close_room.narration: "Nobody else," says Captain Voss. The room is quiet. "Then you had better be right," she says, "and you had better be quick." Pellam writes nothing at all, which he tells you later is the best entry a ledger can have.

choices.label: Hear the real question

scene_told_gatherers_room.narration: "Grandmothers," says Captain Voss, and sighs the sigh of somebody who has argued with grandmothers before. "Very well. They are at least thorough." Pellam writes BELLS in the ledger and underlines it, and somewhere far below, right on cue, one rings.

choices.label: Hear the real question

scene_told_wardens_room.narration: Captain Voss nods once, which is as much as she ever nods. "Then you'll want to know the plan properly," she says, and Pellam opens a fresh ledger with WARDENS AND PARTY on the spine, which he has clearly had ready for some time.

choices.label: Hear the real question

scene_what_for.narration: Then the captain asks the real question. "And you? What is it all for?" Somewhere a stone hums. Everybody in the room is looking at you, and nobody is going to look away first.

choices.label: Put it back. Every stone.
Finish the collection
Take the leash on what's under the mountain
Refuse to say

scene_declared_leash.narration: "The leash," you say. "Hold it. Not break it, not bury it." Captain Voss and Pellam look at each other for a long time. "That is our doctrine," she says slowly, "in a child's words." She does not say whether that is a compliment. Below the window, faintly, somebody at Hessa's soup tent is humming.

choices.label: Hear Pellam read back the record

scene_record_leash.narration: Pellam turns back to the first page. "Maybe you spent the road helping people. Maybe you filled your bags. Maybe you asked who gets to decide," he says. "None of those is the same as holding the leash." He looks up to make sure you hear him. "If the record points another way, you can still choose this one. But you have to know you are choosing." Captain Voss closes the book.

choices.label: Go and find your bunks

scene_declared_hoard.narration: "Finish the collection," you say. The room goes very quiet. Captain Voss does not look angry. She looks like somebody doing arithmetic. "Seven on the table and one in the mountain," she says. "I'll write you down as weather." Pellam writes WEATHER and then, after a moment, puts a question mark after it.

choices.label: Hear Pellam read back the record

scene_record_hoard.narration: Pellam opens the ledger again. "The record may tell a different story," he says. "A kindness done on the road, a question asked, a thing returned. But you have just said collection." He writes COLLECT in his neatest hand, then draws a small question mark beside it. Captain Voss watches the ink dry. "You will have to live up to that word," she says.

choices.label: Go and find your bunks

scene_declared_restore.narration: "Put it back," you say. "Every stone." The Table Stone hums one clear note, as if it heard. Captain Voss does something nobody in the citadel has seen: she unfolds her arms. "Then we'll need every stone that came down," she says. "Tomorrow they start coming back up. Rest."

choices.label: Hear Pellam read back the record

scene_record_restore.narration: Pellam flips back through the record. He reads a line, turns a page, and looks up. "The pages may have pointed somewhere else," he says. "But you are asking to put the stones back. That is what I am writing down." He sets RETURN beside your names and leaves a little space after it, in case the road teaches you something else. Captain Voss watches him write, then nods.

choices.label: Go and find your bunks

scene_undeclared.narration: Nobody says anything. Pellam waits, pen up, then writes it down anyway: no answer means the Reckoning, putting it all back the hard way, with nobody promised to help. "Hardest road there is," says Captain Voss. "Freest, too." She very nearly smiles, and the Table Stone hums as if it approves of the silence.

choices.label: Go and find your bunks

rest_end_ashfall.narration: The wardens give you bunks in a room where every window faces up. Far below, the mountain turns over in its sleep, and every embermoth in the foothills shuffles one step farther away from it. You know what the stones are now, and you know what you want. Rest. Tomorrow, everything you passed on the road comes back up the mountain to meet you.

scene_shut_out.narration: You spend the night outside the gate with the rush's leftovers, while down below the dragonling towns go to bed with their bells on. At midnight a little hatch opens, and a warden clerk called Pellam passes the wardens' old watch-logs out by lantern, one page at a time. Seal. Titan. Rush. "Quickly," he whispers. "What is it all for?"

choices.label: Put it back. Every stone.
Finish the collection
Take the leash on what's under the mountain
Say nothing (Pellam writes down: the Reckoning)

scene_shut_out_refuse.narration: You say nothing. Pellam waits, and the lantern burns, and at last his pen scratches anyway. "The Reckoning, then," he whispers. "Hardest road. Nobody promised." A blanket comes through the hatch, and then, after a moment, a second one.

choices.label: Sleep against the wall

scene_shut_out_leash.narration: "Hold it," you whisper. "The leash." The pen stops. "That's my captain's word," Pellam whispers, sounding puzzled, and passes out a blanket and a very small book with CAGE on the spine, which he asks you to give back in the morning.

choices.label: Sleep against the wall

scene_shut_out_hoard.narration: "Finish the collection," you whisper. There is a pause behind the hatch. "Noted," Pellam whispers at last, and then, after another pause, a blanket comes through anyway.

choices.label: Sleep against the wall

scene_shut_out_restore.narration: "Put it back," you whisper through the hatch. Pellam's pen scratches. "Good," he whispers back, which is not a thing clerks say, and passes out a blanket after the lantern.

choices.label: Sleep against the wall

rest_end_shut_out.narration: You sleep against the cold side of the citadel wall, like the embermoths. The crabs, the sunset and the gate all beat you today, and the mountain noticed: the tremors have settled into a slow, patient rhythm. But the whole truth is in your heads now, and Pellam has left his lantern hanging on the wall for you. It burns all night.

scene_crab_long_way.narration: You back everybody off the warm ground, Dunmore last and grumbling, and take the goat track round the ridge instead. The crab goes back to its pebbles. The goat track is a goat's idea of a road, and by the time it brings you out on the citadel side, the sun is high and the whole morning is gone.

choices.label: Up the ridge road at last

scene_truth_table_charm.narration: You set Mother Thrum's tuned charm on the table. The moment it touches the stone it rings, and the Table Stone rings back, and every warden in the room stops writing at once. Captain Voss waits for the note to die. It takes a long time.

choices.label: Watch it all click together

llmHints.tone: warm, a little spooky, the big reveal told plainly and kindly; grown-ups being rigid or certain, never cruel

npcVoices.hessa: Hessa Wren, Deep Hollow Cult cell contact running a soup tent; warm, generous, remembers every name, completely certain the seal is a cage on the cure
npcVoices.captain: Captain Orla Voss of the Skywardens; rigid, honest, never wastes a word, says 'acceptable losses' as calmly as ordering breakfast
npcVoices.pellam: Pellam, warden clerk; writes everything down twice, proud that the best log entry is 'nothing', secretly kind
npcVoices.grandmother_tull: Grandmother Tull, dragonling bell-keeper; brisk, cozy, says 'nothing to worry about' one time too many
npcVoices.dunmore: Dunmore, a prospector with a pick and no sense; embarrassed easily, means well
npcVoices.claim_pair: two prospectors sharing one humming boulder; stubborn, then sheepish, and hungry the whole time
